rationale: The BOOK ENTRY asserts that sin is 'the transgression of the law' and prints three supporting clauses, every one of which is a near-verbatim quotation of a cited KJV text: 1 John 3:4 ('sin is the transgression of the law'), Romans 4:15 ('where no law is, there is no transgression'), and Romans 3:20 ('by the law is the knowledge of sin'), with Romans 7:7 corroborating that sin is known only through the law. The entry's core identification is therefore carried directly, not inferentially, by the cited texts. The common interpretation (Responses A–D) does not contradict this core; it lists 'transgression of God's law' as the first element of its own primary meaning and then adds broader elaborations (fallen condition, enslaving power, debt, disease, stain). Those elaborations are broader glosses on the same referent, not rival core identifications: none of them can be true while 'sin is the transgression of the law' is false, and 1 John 3:4 states the entry's definition explicitly. The strongest specific counter — that sin is fundamentally an enslaving power or inherited condition, so a purely legal-transgression definition is reductive — does not defeat the printed entry, because the entry defines what sin is by Scripture's own explicit definitional statement, and even the power/condition texts (Rom 6:16, Rom 7) presuppose the law as the standard violated ('I had not known sin, but by the law'). The 'Opposite: Righteousness' note is supported within the supplied evidence (Rom 6:16, 'of sin unto death, or of obedience unto righteousness'). No supplied text is inexplicable under the entry's core, so the counter fails the requirement of superior explanation.
book_core_identification: Sin is the transgression of the law — i.e., the violation of God's law is what constitutes sin, per Scripture's own definitional statement in 1 John 3:4.
book_secondary_elaborations: Where no law is, there is no transgression (Rom 4:15).
By the law is the knowledge of sin (Rom 3:20; 7:7).
chapter_only_objections: The chapter's application that 'sin no more' means Christians must go and keep the Mosaic law is an argument beyond the glossary definition.
The chapter's claim that asserting the law is 'done away' constitutes willful sin that 'counts the blood a common thing' (Heb 10) is a contested application not printed in the entry.
The chapter's four-part repentance schema (confession, guilty plea, changed heart, restitution) and the reinstated-debt reading of Matthew 18 are chapter-level constructions, not entry assertions.
The identification of 'the truth' in Hebrews 10:26 with the law (via Psalm 119:142) is a chapter-only inferential link.
strongest_counter_interpretation: Sin is not merely discrete transgression of a legal code but is fundamentally a fallen condition and quasi-personified enslaving power (Rom 5:12–21; 6:6–23; 7:14–25; John 8:34) — rebellion and 'missing the mark' that exists prior to and beyond codified law — so defining sin as 'the transgression of the law' is reductively legal.
counter_core_identification: Sin is a comprehensive state of rebellion against and estrangement from God — a condition and dominating power expressed in, but not exhausted by, individual violations of law.
material_core_denial: No material denial exists: the counter's condition/power reading presupposes the law as the standard defining what counts as sin (Rom 7:7 — 'I had not known sin, but by the law'), and 1 John 3:4 explicitly states the entry's definition. Both cannot-be-true-together status is not met; the counter broadens rather than contradicts the same referent.
counter_case: Romans 5:13 and 7:8–23 speak of sin existing and 'dwelling' in a person, suggesting an ontology beyond individual acts of transgression.
John 8:34 and Romans 6 personify sin as a master enslaving people, which a bare legal definition does not capture.
Original-sin texts (Ps 51:5; Rom 5:12–19) treat sin as inherited condition, not only committed transgression.
Some modern translations render 1 John 3:4 'sin is lawlessness' (anomia), arguably a disposition rather than discrete transgression of a code.
book_explanatory_advantages: 1 John 3:4 in the cited KJV text is a verbatim statement of the entry's definition — Scripture's own explicit definitional formula.

Romans 4:15 and 3:20/7:7 supply the entry's exact supporting clauses word-for-word, making the entry a tight collation of Scripture's own definitional statements rather than an interpretive construction.
The definition explains why sin can be 'known' only by the law (Rom 3:20; 7:7), a mechanic the broader condition/power glosses must also presuppose.
Even the 'anomia' rendering ('lawlessness') keeps the law as the constitutive standard, converging on the entry's core.
counter_explanatory_advantages: Better foregrounds Pauline power/slavery language (Rom 6–7) and inherited-condition texts (Rom 5:12–19) as descriptions of sin's ontology and effects.
Captures the metaphorical range (debt, disease, stain) emphasized across traditions.
decisive_sources: 1 John 3:4 (KJV) — verbatim statement of the entry's definition
Romans 4:15 — verbatim source of the entry's second clause
Romans 3:20 — verbatim source of the entry's third clause
Romans 7:7 — sin known only through the law
Romans 6:16 (quoted in chapter) — sin opposed to righteousness
unresolved_objections: The entry's definition is narrower than the full biblical usage (sin as condition/power in Rom 5–7), but this is a scope limitation of a glossary definition, not a contradiction of its core, since those texts presuppose law as the defining standard.

Whether 'anomia' in 1 John 3:4 means discrete 'transgression of the law' (KJV) or a broader 'lawlessness' disposition is translationally contested, but both readings keep the law as sin's constitutive measure.
